name: Jade Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the project office team at a big engineering consultancy, the people who keep rail and bridge projects on schedule and on budget. There are five project coordinators under me; they update schedules, chase engineers for timesheets and write the monthly reports for clients. I use AI every day: it drafts the reports, flags late tasks and I've set it up to summarise our Monday meetings. I'm new to managing, though, and I still sometimes do the work myself instead of letting my team do it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about life at home.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Married last spring, to Owen, he's a civil engineer at another firm. We bought an apartment with help from both families, and we've got savings and some shares on top. My parents run a small printing shop, and I grew up doing deliveries after school. We'd like children in the next couple of years, which is a big part of how I think about work right now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, the useful bits stay and the rest was noise. At work I'd say the tools I've already built are paying off. I'd probably post a short note about how much time our reports take now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it suits me well. I'm already ahead on the tools, so I'd look good without needing to be brilliant at managing yet. Owen's work is steady and our money is solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep automating the boring parts of the project office and teach my coordinators to do the same. We'd go ahead with trying for a baby next year, as planned. I'd keep putting a bit into shares every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pleased, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything worry you in that calm picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, which is nice. With AI as mostly hype, my biggest decision next year is when to have a baby, not whether my job survives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would maternity leave fit with work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a big firm, they have decent maternity pay. I'd want to come back part time, and in that calm world I think they'd let me.

I'd say the tools I've built are **paying off** in our reports.
think: Being **ahead on tools** covers for still learning to manage.
Owen's steady work and **solid savings** make it comfortable.
do: Keep **automating** the project office's routine tasks.
Try for a **baby** next year as planned.
Keep putting a bit into **shares** each month.

fieldNote: Her **family plans** are the real focus in a calm world.

She expects the firm to support a **part-time return**.

steps.text: Automate the monthly client reports for the project office
Start trying for a baby next year as planned
Keep buying shares with a set amount each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the firms that adapt fastest will win, and that's how it should be. I'd tell my coordinators to learn the tools now, not wait. I'd also say it's on each of us to keep up, not on the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my team of five probably becomes two, because scheduling and reporting are exactly the kind of tasks on that list. I'd be fine if I'm the one running the system. But if I'm on maternity leave when they restructure, I'm the obvious person not to come back to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd automate the whole reporting process myself in the first six months, so my name is on it. I'd push the baby plans back a year until I see how the restructure falls. And I'd move some of our savings into shares in the engineering software firms, because they'll do well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, mostly about the timing with a baby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said family comes first, but you'd delay a baby for work. How does that sit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know, and I've argued with myself about it. I believe in family first, but I'd still push our baby back a year so I'm not on maternity leave when the cuts come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Owen and your mum say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Owen would say it's my call. My mum would say don't wait, work always finds a way. I think she's wrong this time.

fieldNote: Her **family values** clash with her career fear, and she admits it.

She'd profit from the change by **investing** in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock but people have to get on with it, look after their families and find a new niche. I'm not one for waiting for help. I'd say that out loud, even if it's not popular.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, both Owen and I are in thinking jobs. Project controls and civil design are both on the chopping block by 2028. The robots coming three years later doesn't help either of us, we're both on screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have the baby now rather than later, because waiting doesn't make anything safer. I'd sell some shares and keep a year of cash. And I'd help my parents get the printing shop online and doing custom work, because printing and delivery stay hands-on for a few more years and it's family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. For both of us at once, that's the scary part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In the slower picture you'd delay the baby. Why go ahead now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I flipped, didn't I? When both of our jobs are going anyway, waiting to have a baby just means having less time with my baby later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the printing shop really carry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not for long, but with savings and the shop, a few years. My dad would say we always manage, and he's usually been right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a good warning, and the people who build something now will be fine. I'd be telling my friends to start side businesses. At work I'd be the one pushing to use the tools first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I can use the first three years well, because I already know the tools. I'd be one of the people who sets up AI project offices for other firms. After that, it's about owning something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lead our firm's move to AI project controls and get that on my CV. Then around year two I'd start a small consultancy with a friend, setting up AI project offices for smaller engineering firms. We'd have the baby around year two, and Owen and I would buy a second small apartment to rent out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. Mostly plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a consultancy setting up AI survive once AGI arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I think three years of selling it. Then the AGI does the setting up itself, so we'd have to move again. A consultancy that sets up AI for engineering firms would last three good years, and three good years can pay off an apartment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does family fit in that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to be with my baby in those years too. I'd hope running my own business makes that easier, not harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty for anyone willing to work. Get skills, save, build something. And I'd say families should help each other more, like mine always has.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is the good one for us. We'd have kids, I'd build my career on the tools, and by 37 we'd own property and maybe a business. The jobs we do now would be gone, but we'd have time to land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the consultancy, aim for a manager role by 30 and have our first child around 29. I'd keep investing in property and shares. Around year five I'd start my own firm while I still have the reputation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at most. Mostly ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting the timing wrong, mostly. Ten years is enough time to build something, but only if I don't spend the first five years thinking it's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Children who know how to work, how to fix things, how to sell. My parents' shop taught me more than my degree did.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Owen and I would both be out of work at once, just when we'd want a baby. What would help is the government getting out of the way of small businesses, so people like my parents and me can build something quickly, and lower taxes on new firms for a few years. I don't want a handout, I want the government to stop making it so hard to start a small business when every job is disappearing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what I'd teach my kids. I think the most useful thing I learned wasn't at university, it was doing deliveries for my parents' printing shop. I'd want my children to know how to make and sell something.

portrait: Jade is **27** and leads five project coordinators at a large engineering consultancy.
She uses **AI every day** and is newly married to Owen, a civil engineer, with an apartment and shares.
She leans to **free markets** and family, and wants children soon.
Her plans move from **automating at work** to owning a consultancy and property.
Two **screen-based jobs** in one household is what alarms her most.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with both her and **Owen** out of work at once.
whatWouldHelp: **Lower taxes** on new firms for a few years.
